text: A bad application deployment is usually recoverable in seconds — roll back to the previous build and the old version comes right back. A bad terraform apply is a different kind of risk. It can delete a production database, replace a VPC other resources depend on, or rewrite a security group in a way that locks out real traffic, and some of that isn't simply reversible by redeploying something. That's why Lesson 25 put plan on autopilot but apply stays gated behind a person.

GitHub Actions has a built-in mechanism for exactly this: an environment. The trigger, on push to the main branch, still fires automatically on every merge — but environment: production is the one line that stops apply from actually running the moment that happens. It ties the job to a GitHub Environment configured under Settings, Environments, where Required reviewers is turned on. The job pauses, showing Waiting for review, until a named person approves it.

A repository admin sets that reviewer list once — either in the Settings UI, or with one gh api call naming the user by id against the production environment. Every subsequent workflow run that targets that environment inherits the rule automatically from then on. Nothing in the workflow file itself needs to change once it's configured; the gate lives on the environment, not on the pipeline definition.

Put the pieces in order and the shape is simple: a merge to main starts the job, the job pauses waiting for review because environment: production has required reviewers, a named reviewer approves it in the GitHub UI, and only then does terraform apply -auto-approve actually execute. Terraform Cloud enforces the identical shape its own way — a workspace set to Manual Apply pauses every run after plan until a person clicks Confirm & Apply.

Either platform, the principle doesn't change: the trigger for apply can stay fully automatic, but the apply itself never runs unattended — a real person has to look and say yes first. Next, that apply step still needs real cloud credentials to actually do anything. Lesson 27 covers where those credentials should live, and how to keep a sensitive Terraform output from printing in the log right next to them.
